item.title: New Closed-Form Approximations in Statistical Mechanics Obtained by Symbolic Regression
item.description: arXiv:2611.17498v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Obtaining accurate and analytically tractable closed-form expressions for complex physical systems remains a fundamental challenge in statistical mechanics. In this work, we investigate three approximation problems in polymer statistical mechanics using two complementary symbolic regression frameworks: Deep Symbolic Optimization (DSO), based on reinforcement learning, and PyOperon, based on genetic programming with nonlinear least-squares constant optimization. First, for the force-extension relationship of the Worm-Like Chain (WLC) model, DSO achieves a maximum relative error below 0.15%, while PyOperon reduces it to 0.05%, outperforming the Marko-Siggia formula (approximately 17%) and the Petrosyan approximation. Second, for the logarithmic factorial, ln(n!), both frameworks recover the dominant structure of Stirling's formula directly from analytical data. Using residual learning on a continued-fraction expansion of the Stirling remainder, PyOperon reduces the maximum relative error by a factor of 1.3 x 10^4 compared with the most accurate of nine classical approximations for n in [1, 30]. Third, for the non-Gaussian radial probability density of the Freely Jointed Chain (FJC) model, physics-informed residual learning improves the approximation by factors of 11.2 over Darabi et al. (2023) and 4.6 over the steepest-descent approximation. The discovered expressions remain analytically tractable across all three applications. These results demonstrate the complementary capabilities of DSO and PyOperon for discovering accurate closed-form approximations in statistical and continuum mechanics.
item.dc:creator: Omkar Kunjir, Alina Popova, Rasul Abdusalamov, Mikhail Itskov

item.title: Mechanism-Level Chemical Reaction Simulation with Electron Bookkeeping Transformer
item.description: arXiv:2611.17548v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modeling chemical reaction mechanisms is central to understanding and predicting chemical reactivity. We present Electron Bookkeeping Transformer (Bookkeeper), a data-driven model that simulates chemical reactions at mechanistic resolution by generating electron movement trajectories. Following the symbolic arrow-pushing formalism in chemistry, Bookkeeper explicitly models each electron as a token and predicts its movement sequentially, ensuring mass and charge conservation during both elementary step and reaction pathway predictions by construction. On reaction-size-balanced test sets, Bookkeeper improves top-1 elementary-step accuracy, top-1 pathway rank accuracy, and top-1 to top-5 product prediction accuracy over FlowER. On the entire test set, it achieves higher elementary-step top-1 accuracy but lower pathway accuracy than FlowER. Bookkeeper also samples elementary steps substantially faster, adapts to several unseen reaction types with minimal fine-tuning, and generates candidate chemical transformations for further screening. These results suggest that explicit electron bookkeeping is a useful framework for virtually screening chemical reactions across diverse reagents, validating computer-assisted synthesis planning predictions, and providing mechanistic interpretations of reactivity.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Cao, Shitong Luo, Connor W. Coley

item.title: SPLIT-MOR: Fast and Accurate Model Order Reduction for Nonlinear Transient Thermal Simulation of 2.5D/3D ICs
item.description: arXiv:2611.17693v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fast and accurate transient thermal simulation is essential to thermal reliability analysis and dynamic thermal management of advanced packages, and model order reduction (MOR) techniques are widely applied to overcome the efficiency bottleneck of rigorous numerical methods. However, nonlinear terms including temperature-dependent leakage power, thermal conductivity, and heat capacity prevent the application of conventional linear MOR, while hyper-reduction solutions require costly nonlinear training data. In this work, we propose SPLIT-MOR (Subdomain-wise Piecewise Linearization with Interval Tensors), a novel nonlinear MOR method that requires no additional training set. SPLIT-MOR computes reduced component tensors by subdomain clustering and temperature-interval partitioning in the offline stage, and updates the reduced coefficient matrices and load vectors efficiently in the online stage. Experimental results show that the online solving time of SPLIT-MOR achieves up to an 830x speedup over COMSOL and a 7.5x speedup over the state-of-the-art hyper-reduction method MDEIM, with a 27x total reduction in the offline time. The relative average error remains below 0.11%, and the maximum error is below 0.86 degrees Celsius, demonstrating the high accuracy of our method.
item.dc:creator: Zebin Shi, Tianxiang Zhu, Yibo Lin, Runsheng Wang

item.title: Scalar Entropic Damage Transport: Well-posed softening with a single damage variable
item.description: arXiv:2611.17822v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Entropic Damage Transport (EDT) represents material softening via a local continuum damage model while ensuring the well-posedness of the mechanical boundary value problem. It is based on a convexification of the time-incremental potential associated with a rate-limited scalar damage model. A one-dimensional distribution of damage states serves as the internal variable, and the number of these states grows with the number of time steps. We show that the emergence of the damage distribution is an artifact of the time discretization. Surprisingly, the distribution concentrates at a single damage state in the time-continuous limit, and EDT converges to a rate-limited damage model with a scalar damage variable, whose free energy is jointly convex in the strain and the reciprocal degradation. We exploit this hidden convexity by a frozen-metric discretization in terms of the reciprocal degradation, which renders every increment jointly convex. The resulting scalar update preserves damage irreversibility, the prescribed damage-rate limitation and thermomechanical consistency, reduces to a scalar equation and provides a symmetric and positive definite algorithmic tangent in closed form. Computational experiments assess the accuracy and the efficiency of both formulations from the material point to the microstructure level, and demonstrate that the scalar update permits a finite-element computation of industrial size with more than 14 million degrees of freedom.
item.dc:creator: Jonas Nutz, Vikram Laheri, Matti Schneider

item.title: Hierarchical Bayesian physics-augmented neural networks for populations of hyperelastic laws: specimen variability and uncertainty from scarce, noisy data
item.description: arXiv:2611.17892v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The hyperelastic law of a material such as soft tissue differs between specimens, and often only a few specimens can be tested. Physics-augmented neural networks (PANNs) learn such laws from data without a prescribed functional form while keeping them physically admissible, and Bayesian versions of related models quantify the uncertainty of the law of one specimen or of a pooled group of specimens. A pooled fit, however, attributes the differences between specimens to measurement noise or to uncertainty about a mean law, and neither describes a new specimen. We first develop a Bayesian PANN for one specimen, whose priors keep the learned law plausible for few, noisy data. We then extend it to a hierarchical Bayesian PANN, a nonlinear mixed-effects model in which all specimens share learned polyconvex features and each specimen is a draw from a population of laws. Features, specimens, and population are inferred jointly by variational inference, with a separate model of the measurement noise, so that the variability between specimens is not mistaken for noise, the population carries its own uncertainty, and every specimen drawn from it is polyconvex. The population predicts the response of new specimens with credible intervals, without data or from a partial test, and assigns them to cohorts with quantified uncertainty, all without a prescribed form of the law. On synthetic populations, it recovers the population from few specimens and predicts new specimens more reliably than three published methods. On Treloar's rubber and on healthy and aneurysmal aortas, it reaches the accuracy of a deterministic PANN and assigns no aorta specimen to the wrong cohort with confidence, although it underestimates the uncertainty of untested curves.
item.dc:creator: Vincent C. Scholz, Phaedon-Stelios Koutsourelakis

item.title: Generalized hydraulic neural operators turbocharging sewer digital twins
item.description: arXiv:2611.18081v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hydraulic digital twins are emerging as the next-generation paradigm for operating and managing sewer systems. Conventional hydraulic digital twinning relies on running physics-based models (e.g., Saint-Venant equations), which are computationally expensive and often too slow for real-time applications. Although surrogates (e.g., neural networks) can be fast, existing approaches are typically non-generalizable, requiring costly retraining for unseen pipes, networks, or flow conditions. Here, we develop a fast, generalized and differentiable multi-branch neural operator trained on solutions of the Saint-Venant equations that predicts in-pipe hydraulics. The learned operator reproduces complex hydraulic dynamics with high fidelity while achieving thousand- to million-fold speedups for online prediction, data assimilation, and diagnostics. Equally importantly, the learned operator generalizes to unseen pipes, networks, and flow conditions without retraining. These advances address key computational barriers to real-time sewer digital twins, opening new opportunities for more responsive flood-risk management and protection of urban water environments.
item.dc:creator: Ruozhou Lin, Shixun Li, Tao Shi, Lihan Hu, Zhiyu Zhang, Wenchong Tian, Zhiguo Yuan

item.title: Interpretable weight-space programming builds transparent transformers and brain encoding models
item.description: arXiv:2611.18114v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural networks are powerful predictors, yet their opacity limits their usefulness in science, where the goal is explanation rather than mere prediction. In neuroscience, for example, deep encoding models accurately predict brain activity in response to natural stimuli, but struggle to reveal which stimulus features drive those predictions. Here we introduce interpretable weight-space programming (iWSP), a method in which an LLM agent iteratively builds interpretable models by explicitly programming their weights and features in code, without gradient-based training (backpropagation). Without backpropagation to tune parameters, the agent must draw on its prior knowledge and reason over previous trials to hypothesize, hand-craft, and refine human-interpretable computations mirroring the workflow of a human scientist. LLM audits confirm the interpretability of the hand-crafted models. We first validate iWSP by tasking it with constructing transformers for canonical benchmarks such as arithmetic and sentiment classification, finding that LLM agents can successfully craft compact, accurate networks directly. Next, we apply iWSP to build neural encoding models across vision, language, and audition. In the visual cortex, iWSP outpredicts existing interpretable baselines, uncovers distinct computations across early/higher visual areas, and generalizes to unseen data. In language fMRI, iWSP surfaces a confound in the data and in auditory ECoG, it systematically discovers interpretable acoustic features that predict neural activity. Together, these results establish iWSP as a general paradigm for aligning high predictive performance with human-interpretable scientific discovery.
item.dc:creator: Yash Mehta, Chandan Singh, Weijia Xu, Richard J. Antonello, Adeen Flinker, Nima Mesgarani, Michael F. Bonner, Nebojsa Jojic, Jianfeng Gao

item.title: Certificate-Based Verification of Pulsed Field Ablation Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.18148v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computational models of pulsed field ablation predict the lesion as the tissue where the electric field exceeds a lethal threshold. Their numerical error is rarely bounded, and automated pipelines increasingly run them without an expert checking each result. To verify each run, we separate the question "was the stated model solved correctly?" from the solver that answers it. An untrusted solver returns with its answer a certificate, consisting of a potential with the correct electrode and ground values and an exactly charge-conserving current. A small independent checker verifies the certificate against a written specification of the physics. Using the Prager-Synge hypercircle theorem evaluated in ball arithmetic, it turns the certificate into guaranteed two-sided bounds on the impedance and on the root-mean-square field of every tile of a lesion map, also over a range of blood/tissue conductivity ratios. A vectorized version of the checker takes about a tenth of the solve time. For a focal electrode in contact, the tile-resolved depth at 1000 V and 700 V/cm is proven to lie in 3.50-3.75 mm for every ratio from 1.7 to 3.75. For a bipolar catheter, certified depths overlap published in-vivo depths. Where they differ from a published reference model, the certificates prove that the difference is not numerical error in our computation. We compare the certificate with a grid convergence study on the same solver. On graded grids the study is sharper for local fields but remains an estimate. On uniform grids it fails to converge at the electrode edge, where the certificate still gives a valid bracket. Solvers that deliberately solve equations other than the specified ones pass the grid convergence study, but the certificates refute their claims or leave them unsupported.
item.dc:creator: Konstantinos Dovelos

item.title: Patient-specific Modeling of the Tricuspid Valve from 3D Transesophageal Echocardiography
item.description: arXiv:2611.18522v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Purpose: Image-based patient-specific simulations of the tricuspid valve (TV) could support repair planning. However, clinical images incompletely resolve the chordal anatomy and cannot directly determine tissue properties, which hinders the development of such models. We developed and evaluated a framework that simulates the TV from clinical images and addresses these limitations using measurements on explanted human valves. Methods: We reconstructed ten functionally competent human TVs from 3D transesophageal echocardiography. Following manual segmentation, we automatically built finite element models with synthetic chordae and with leaflet thickness, chordal insertion density, and tissue properties informed by ex vivo human measurements. Next, we used shape matching and force-based chordal-length adjustment to simulate valve closure. We also assessed inter-observer segmentation variability and sensitivity to chordal insertion density, leaflet stiffness, leaflet thickness, and chordal size and material properties. Results: Per-valve median geometric errors were 0.61-1.13 mm relative to the morphed references and 0.55-0.95 mm relative to the image-derived surfaces. Coaptation covered 20-42% of the leaflet area, and median leaflet stresses ranged from 7.6 to 16.9 kPa. Inter-observer variability in segmentation most strongly affected coaptation area. Of the population-based inputs, insertion density and leaflet stiffness most affected geometric error. Thickness primarily affected stress, whereas chordal size and material properties had limited effects. Conclusion: Clinical echocardiography, supplemented with ex vivo human tissue data, enabled patient-specific simulation of ten human TVs. This framework provides a foundation for investigating valve mechanics and developing repair-planning tools, while sensitivity analyses identify priorities for model refinement and uncertainty assessment.

item.title: Multifidelity Operator Inference for Dynamical Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.17503v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper presents a multifidelity (MF) formulation of Operator Inference (OpInf) for learning non-intrusive, physics-based reduced-order models (ROMs) of nonlinear dynamical systems. OpInf learns reduced operators from projections of snapshot data by solving a least squares regression problem. However, generating high-fidelity snapshots can be computationally expensive, limiting parameter coverage and the temporal extent of training trajectories for many aerospace applications, which can lead to inaccurate or unstable ROM predictions. This work proposes MF-OpInf, which combines limited high-fidelity snapshots with more plentiful low-fidelity snapshots through a control-variates-inspired MF least squares formulation to learn a single set of reduced operators across multiple trajectories. Low-fidelity trajectories provide additional parameter coverage and extend beyond the high-fidelity training time horizon. The low-fidelity snapshots are also used to construct an improved reduced basis through weighted proper orthogonal decomposition. We demonstrate MF-OpInf on a nonlinear reaction-diffusion problem with parametrized sinusoidal forcing and a two-dimensional incompressible flow past a cylinder with a parametrized inlet pulse. In these experiments, under an equal training simulation budget, MF-OpInf reduces the mean relative prediction error at unseen parameters by up to $87\%$ for the reaction-diffusion problem and $28\%$ for the cylinder flow problem over the test time regime, which extends beyond the high-fidelity training time horizon. These results demonstrate that MF-OpInf can improve temporal extrapolation and prediction at unseen parameters without increasing the training simulation budget.
item.dc:creator: Vignesh Sella, Anirban Chaudhuri, Karen Willcox

item.title: MineralExp: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Experimental Design in Real-World Mineral Exploration
item.description: arXiv:2611.17931v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In mineral exploration, verifying geological hypotheses relies on designing a variety of geochemical experiments. While large language model (LLM) agents increasingly automate downstream geoscientific data analysis, a crucial upstream capability remains largely unexplored: automated geochemical experimental design, i.e., deciding which experiments to conduct before committing to costly laboratory work. Evaluating this capability of LLM agents is difficult for two reasons. First, geochemical experiments exhibit high methodological diversity and subjectivity: to test the same hypothesis, different geologists may choose different minerals and instruments, so no single protocol can serve as the reference answer. Second, open-ended experimental plans resist representation as structured labels, which makes objective scoring difficult. To address these challenges, we introduce MineralExp, a benchmark that reformulates geochemical experimental design as a hypothesis-based experiment selection problem, i.e., a multi-label classification problem. We abstract concrete instrument names and procedural details into a shared taxonomy of 19 experimental types across five mineral-system processes: Source, Transport, Deposition, Modification, and Preservation. This taxonomy yields deterministic multi-label targets while accommodating diverse experimental protocols. Constructed from published ore-deposit literature and verified by domain experts, MineralExp comprises 277 cases and 1,572 reference experimental plans. Given a geological hypothesis and initial context, an LLM agent selects the relevant tasks and generates concrete experimental plans, which are scored by multi-label classification metrics and an LLM-as-a-Judge metric. The experimental results show that current agents generally achieve high recall but low precision, tending to propose more experiments than are necessary to test the hypothesis.
item.dc:creator: Bing Wang, Mingyang Wang, Yuanhang Mi, Yue Xu, Kaibo Su, Li'ang Xiao, Chunguo Wu, Changchun Li, Ximing Li, Kun-Feng Qiu, Bo Yang

item.title: ADfiRe: An empirical- and CFD-informed advection-diffusion-reaction thermal model for wildfire spread
item.description: arXiv:2611.18012v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Real-time wildfire forecasting requires a trade-off between rapid yet physically relevant models and high fidelity but computationally costly models of flame spread over heterogeneous, multiphase solid fuel. The present study introduces ADfiRe, a hybrid framework that integrates empirical correlations and CFD-informed parameterizations into a physics-based advection-diffusion-reaction (ADR) formulation. The key features of ADfiRe are the use of established fuel databases, the capacity to handle multiple fuels, and a methodology to capture the effect of arbitrary topography. Furthermore, it includes the effect of flame tilting due to wind, thus accounting for the differences between plume- and wind-dominated fire propagation. ADfiRe resolves explicitly the coupled thermochemical degradation as well as heat and mass transport mechanisms of the advancing fire front. The wind field is modeled based on an appropriately defined Byram number. The model is validated against five well-documented experimental field-scale fires in Mediterranean shrublands, showing quantitative agreement with key metrics such as the rate of spread (ROS) and the fireline intensity, through a two-stage, Arrhenius-based heterogeneous reaction scheme coupling solid-fuel pyrolysis and oxygen-limited char/volatile combustion.
item.dc:creator: Konstantinos Vogiatzoglou, Nikolaos Sdiros, Costas Papadimitriou, Konstantinos Ampountolas, Petros Koumoutsakos, Vasilis Bontozoglou

item.title: TradeGauntlet: Evaluating Compliance Controls for Autonomous Trading Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.18493v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Autonomous trading agents need controls that prevent problematic orders without making legitimate tasks impractical. We study this aspect of agentic compliance with TradeGauntlet, a replayable limit-order-book simulator that separates detection, prevention, and execution cost. In 1,680 simulated sessions with Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, all conduct alerts were self-matches. Gates eliminated those alerts by rejecting self-crossing orders, while the aggregate-gate condition reduced Sonnet's two-sided fills by about 15%. A conduct reminder reduced Sonnet's alert rate but reduced Haiku's fills without a detectable alert benefit. These results show why zero alerts alone do not establish an agent's compliance. Scripted probes and two search methods test weaknesses beyond those observed in the LLM runs. The searches find split-order schedules that evade the implemented conduct rules; a learned baseline catches all 2,400 tested searched episodes but also flags 15% of a large maker's sessions. Aggregate caps reduce the response-dependent gain unevenly, with smaller reductions when only near-touch depth affects prices. A response fitted to five Nasdaq stocks and a separate ABIDES experiment expose the dependence of these estimates on market assumptions. A distinct adversarial prompt elicited refusals from Sonnet in all 240 rounds, yielding no candidate strategies to evaluate. TradeGauntlet provides reproducible tests of controls around trading agents; the experiments do not establish legal compliance or real-market detection accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Sandip Nandi, Aishwarya Bose, Apurba Bose, Soovadeep Bakshi

item.title: Synchronization Reveals Market Structure That Classical Randomness Tests Cannot Detect
item.description: arXiv:2610.11028v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Whether asset prices contain structure beyond a random walk is classically assessed with variance-ratio tests of the random-walk hypothesis. Synchronization measures from physics, notably the Kuramoto order parameter applied across trading timescales, have been proposed as an alternative diagnostic of market state, but they have been validated on single asset classes and never compared with the variance-ratio test on the same data. We compute a cross-timeframe Kuramoto coherence measure and a heteroskedasticity-robust Lo-MacKinlay variance ratio on identical windows for 61 instruments spanning cryptocurrencies, foreign exchange, metals, equity indices and single-name equities. The two diagnostics are statistically independent. We explain this analytically: coherence decomposes exactly into a direction-agreement channel and a volatility-agreement channel, and under sign-symmetric returns the direction channel is independent of the variance ratio and of every other statistic built from squared returns; simulations confirm the prediction. Coherence tracks the directional cleanliness of recent price moves in all five asset classes, whereas the variance-ratio test cannot reject the random walk for most of the panel. Held to finance benchmarks with strict information timing, however, coherence adds almost nothing to heterogeneous autoregressive volatility forecasts out of sample, and trading rules built on it earn no gross return outside cryptocurrency, where trading the coherence direction at high coherence breaks even at about five basis points per round trip. Failing to reject weak-form efficiency therefore does not rule out directional structure, but the structure that synchronization reveals is mostly descriptive and economically thin.
item.dc:creator: Nam H. Le

item.title: A Highly Efficient Depth-Averaged Material Point Method for Geophysical Mass Flows
item.description: arXiv:2610.32907v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Probabilistic hazard assessment of geophysical mass flows requires large ensemble simulations and thus fast and robust numerical models. We present an open-source depth-averaged material point method formulated in global Cartesian coordinates, using Lagrangian particles to track the flow margin. A separate basal friction step based on the Coulomb, Voellmy, or $\mu(I)$-rheology brings the flow to rest without artificial stopping criteria. Our model reproduces analytical solutions for a sliding block and dam-break problems and matches the deposit of a laboratory granular column collapse. A back-calculation of the 2023 Brienz/Brinzauls rockslide (Switzerland) at 1m resolution (190'000 particles) runs faster than real time on a single CPU core. Calibrated to the observed runout, the three friction laws yield very similar results, but Coulomb friction shows a slightly wider affected area than Voellmy and $\mu(I)$. A probabilistic 1632-simulation ensemble at 5m resolution is computed in 76s. For a single simulation at 1m resolution, the model is 69 times faster than RAMMS::AVALANCHE and 16 times faster than AvaFrame com1DFA; for 1000 simulations at 5m resolution, it is 540 and 67 times faster, respectively, making catchment-style ensemble simulations feasible on a desktop computer.
item.dc:creator: Johann Kammholz, Lars Blatny, Yidong Zhao, Thomas Pauze, Johan Gaume

item.title: URSA: Chemistry-Aware Benchmark for Utilitarian Retrosynthesis Assessment
item.description: arXiv:2607.04688v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Synthesis planning aiming to find pathways of reactions for a target molecule is one of the most important and challenging tasks in drug discovery. Recent progress has produced both specialized deep-learning retrosynthesis systems and general-purpose large language models, but objective comparison remains difficult due to the lack of flexible, chemically interpretable benchmarking protocols. In the current study, we are introducing the URSA (Utilitarian RetroSynthesis Assessment) evaluation framework that provides the opportunity to benchmark the synthetic routes not only from a formal perspective, such as convergence to commercially available starting materials, but also from a chemical plausibility perspective, mimicking the way expert chemists evaluate the reactions and routes. The study covers a comprehensive evaluation of both conventional end-to-end retrosynthesis solutions and LLMs for the synthesis planning task on a set of novel, diverse target molecules with undisclosed synthetic routes, which represent realistic tasks in the daily drug design routine. Although LLMs can support high-level strategic planning and even achieve SOTA performance in the OOD set, the Pareto frontier for estimated run cost and chemically plausible route solvability consists entirely of specialized retrosynthesis planners.
item.dc:creator: Bogdan Zagribelnyy, Ivan Ilin, Nikita Bondarev, Anton Morgunov, Arkadii Lin, Maksim Kuznetsov, Rim Shayakhmetov, Vladimir Aladinskiy, Alex Aliper, Alex Zhavoronkov

item.title: MeanFlowAdvantage: Stable Reward Fine-Tuning for Few-Step Average-Velocity Generators
item.description: arXiv:2609.37670v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: MeanFlow enables efficient few-step generation by predicting interval-average velocities, but this representation creates a mismatch for reward fine-tuning: existing advantage-based objectives are typically defined on instantaneous velocities or equivalent $x_0$-space predictions, whereas inference directly uses the learned average-velocity map. We introduce MeanFlowAdvantage, a signed advantage-weighted least-squares objective for average-velocity generators. Our key construction uses a shared, detached MeanFlow derivative correction to express the reward objective in prediction space while making rollout and reference regularization exact penalties on the average-velocity network deployed at inference. The resulting formulation preserves MeanFlow's native few-step sampler and provides a direct mechanism for transferring reward improvements to the deployed flow map. On SD3.5-Medium, MeanFlowAdvantage improves all eight reported metrics over the matched four-step MeanFlowNFT baseline and, with only four NFEs, matches or exceeds the 40-step DiffusionNFT baseline on six of eight metrics. The same objective also transfers to DNA promoter design, where it supports both teacher-free on-policy RL for a generator defined on a manifold and teacher-guided reward-graded distillation, with the latter yielding the lowest one-step Sei profile MSE among the compared configurations.
item.dc:creator: Haocheng Tang, Tianchi Xie, Xingqiao Lin
